962: Protons return to the matrix by spinning the rotor of ATP synthase. Each full turn makes three ATP from ADP and phosphate.
963: The H⁺ flow turns the c-ring (8 subunits in mammals) and the γ shaft inside the F1 head, whose three β sites cycle through the open, loose and tight states (Boyer). 8 H⁺ for 3 ATP, plus 1 H⁺ per ATP to import phosphate. Inhibited by oligomycin.
964: How many protons for one full turn in mammals?
966: Four reactions that repeat: at each round the fatty acid loses two carbons as acetyl-CoA. Example with an 8-carbon chain.
967: Each round: 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA. Palmitate (C16) gives 8 acetyl-CoA in 7 rounds, i.e. ≈ 106 net ATP.
969: Two hydrogens are removed between carbons 2 and 3 of the fatty acid: a double bond appears, FAD is reduced.
970: Enzymes specific for a chain length (VLCAD, MCAD, SCAD). FADH₂ gives its electrons to ETF, then to ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase. MCAD deficiency, screened at birth, causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia on fasting.
971: To what does acyl-CoA dehydrogenase pass its electrons?
976: A water molecule adds across the double bond: an –OH group appears on carbon 3.
977: Stereospecific hydration giving L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA. For long chains, this activity and the next two are carried by the trifunctional protein of the inner membrane (HADHA/HADHB).
978: On which carbon is the hydroxyl placed?
983: The –OH group is oxidised to a ketone; NAD⁺ picks up two electrons.
984: Deficiency of the long-chain activity (LCHAD) of the trifunctional protein combines cardiomyopathy and retinopathy, and exposes the mother of an affected fetus to acute fatty liver of pregnancy.
985: Which coenzyme is reduced at this step?
990: A coenzyme A cuts the chain: one acetyl-CoA comes off, and the fatty acid, two carbons shorter, goes round again.
991: Thiolysis: the thiol of CoA attacks carbon 3. In the fasting hepatocyte, excess acetyl-CoA is converted into ketone bodies (mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase).
992: How many rounds to oxidise palmitate (C16)?
994: Eight enzymes, between mitochondrion and cytosol. The erythroblast makes it its speciality: it needs one haem per globin chain.
995: 8 glycines and 8 succinyl-CoA for one haem; enough to equip ≈ 270 million haemoglobin molecules per cell.
997: It all starts in the mitochondrion: a glycine and a succinyl-CoA are assembled into δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA).
998: Erythroid form, using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6): the rate-limiting step. Its mRNA carries a 5′ IRE element: without iron its translation is blocked. Its mutations cause X-linked sideroblastic anaemia.
999: Which cofactor does ALA synthase use?
1001: In the cytosol, two ALA are joined into a five-membered ring, porphobilinogen: this is the “pyrrole” building block.
1002: Porphobilinogen synthase, a zinc enzyme. Lead displaces the zinc and inhibits it: ALA builds up, which explains part of the signs of lead poisoning.
1003: Which toxic agent inhibits ALA dehydratase?
1007: HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX, PPOX (five steps summarised)
1008: Four pyrroles are linked then closed into a large ring, whose side chains are retouched. The product, back in the mitochondrion, is protoporphyrin IX.
1009: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase (4 NH₃ released), uroporphyrinogen III synthase (closure with inversion of ring D), uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (4 CO₂), then, in the mitochondrion, coproporphyrinogen oxidase (2 CO₂) and protoporphyrinogen oxidase. Each deficiency causes a porphyria.
1010: How many pyrroles make up a porphyrin?
1012: Last step: an iron atom is inserted at the centre of protoporphyrin. Haem is ready to join a globin chain.
1013: On the matrix face of the inner membrane; Fe²⁺ is imported by mitoferrin 1. Without iron, zinc is inserted instead (zinc protoporphyrin). Free haem slows its own synthesis and, via the kinase HRI, coordinates globin translation.
1014: Which metal is inserted when iron is lacking?
1019: The hepatocyte turns ammonia, toxic to the brain, into urea. Two steps in the mitochondrion, three in the cytosol.
1020: NH₃ + HCO₃⁻ + aspartate + 3 ATP → urea + fumarate. An adult excretes 20 to 30 g of urea per day.
1022: In the mitochondrion, ammonia is fixed onto bicarbonate, at the cost of two ATP: carbamoyl phosphate.
1023: Rate-limiting step, active only in the presence of N-acetylglutamate, itself made when amino acids are plentiful. Its deficiency causes neonatal hyperammonaemia.
1024: What is the obligatory activator of CPS1?
1029: The carbamoyl group is transferred onto ornithine: citrulline is born and leaves the mitochondrion.
1030: Its X-linked deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder; excess carbamoyl phosphate spills over into pyrimidine synthesis, hence orotic aciduria.
1031: Which urinary sign accompanies OTC deficiency?
1036: In the cytosol, aspartate brings the second nitrogen atom of the future urea.
1037: Citrulline is activated as citrullyl-AMP, then attacked by the amine of aspartate. Hydrolysis of pyrophosphate makes the reaction irreversible. Its deficiency is citrullinaemia type I.
1038: Where does the second nitrogen of urea come from?
1043: Argininosuccinate is split into arginine and fumarate, which returns to the Krebs cycle.
1044: Fumarate, converted to malate then oxaloacetate, can give aspartate again by transamination: the two cycles are coupled.
1045: Which product links this cycle to the Krebs cycle?
1049: Arginase releases urea, which will travel in the blood to the kidneys, and regenerates ornithine for another turn.
1050: A manganese enzyme of periportal hepatocytes. Two nitrogens eliminated for 3 ATP used, i.e. 4 high-energy bonds.
1055: A tree of sugars is grafted onto the nascent protein, then pruned: each form is a message read by chaperones. Colours: GlcNAc dark blue, mannose green, glucose light blue.
1056: 14 sugars transferred, 3 glucoses and 1 mannose removed: Man₈GlcNAc₂ on a folded protein, ready for the Golgi.
1058: As soon as the protein enters the reticulum, a tree of 14 sugars pre-assembled on a lipid is transferred in one piece onto an asparagine.
1059: The catalytic subunit STT3A, next to the translocon, recognises the sequon Asn-X-Ser/Thr (X ≠ Pro) and links the first GlcNAc to the amide nitrogen. The donor is assembled by the ALG enzymes, whose deficiencies are CDGs. Tunicamycin blocks its first step.
1063: At once, a first glucose is removed from the tip of the tree.
1064: Hydrolysis of the terminal α1-2-linked glucose (gene MOGS; its deficiency is a CDG). The two-glucose glycan is recognised by malectin.
